newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to extend British pub, petrol station rules.
newsitem.headline: EU to extend British pub, petrol station rules.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday will extend until the end of the century two block exemptions regulation allowing British breweries and the oil industry to run exclusive distribution and purchasing agreements.

At the same time, it will adopt its long-awaited Green Paper on Vertical Restraints to help it define future policy on such deals as well as franchise agreements which have mushroomed in the past 10 years in the clothing, perfume and hotel industries.

The delay in finalising the consultation document is why it has to extend the two regulations which allow British breweries to operate tied public houses (inns) and oil companies to conclude exclusive purchasing agreements with petrol stations.
The regulations, 1983/83 and 1984/83, would normally expire at the end of 1997.

"We welcome the extension," James Wilson, Public Affairs Executive at British brewery Bass Plc told Reuters, adding: "It's a step in the right direction, but obviously we expect the tie to continue for much longer."
British pubs are mostly owned by breweries which restrict tenants to selling their own brands and those of one competitor.
The oil industry has also insisted that its exemption must be extended, possibly by as long as 10 years renewable, as the only way to ensure the legal certainty needed for long-term investment.
Industry sources and diplomats said the Commission's paper left all options open. "It does not really angle towards one scenario or another," one diplomat said.
The Commission currently grants block exemptions from article 85 of the EC treaty to sectoral agreements, even if they contain anti-competitive provisions, provided consumers benefit.
It must decide, after consulting with all interested parties, whether to carry on with the existing policy, to tighten it or make it more lax.
Whatever new rules it comes up with, they are not expected to be adopted for at least a year because of the wide-ranging implications for just about every commercial sector.
